title: Relapsing Fever and Leptospirosis: Catching the Corkscrew at the Right Time
summary: Recognise spirochetes by their hidden periplasmic flagella, diagnose relapsing fever with blood films taken during a fever bout (GlpQ antibodies point to relapsing-fever Borrelia rather than Lyme Borrelia), and match leptospirosis specimens to the week of illness: blood first, urine from week two, paired sera to confirm.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 61 Hits 11 (relapsing fever: blood microscopy during febrile episodes; GlpQ) and 12 (leptospirosis phases, specimen timing, Weil disease) and the chapter figure (corkscrew spirochete with endoflagella), checked against Jakab 2022, Warrell 2019, Trevisan 2021, Schwan 1996 (abstract only), Nakamura 2020, Haake & Levett 2015 (NIH author manuscript, full text via NCBI), Sykes 2022 and Goarant 2016. Qualifications: Goarant 2016 reports that the Weil triad accounts for under one-third of confirmed leptospirosis cases and that the biphasic fever is not systematically observed (lesson flag; proposed register flag rv-lepto-biphasic-weil-context). Not taught (pending): the reviewer’s “34-kDa” size for GlpQ (Schwan 1996 abstract reports a 39-kDa immunoreactive clone protein), blood culture “in the first 10 days”, urine “up to 30 days”, “bacteremic 4–7 days”, and “1–50%” Weil mortality; Number Vault rows; Exam Traps not involved.

objectives: Describe the spirochete body plan, with flagella inside the periplasmic space, and name the main spirochete pathogens.
Choose the right specimen and timing for relapsing fever (blood films during a febrile episode) and explain what GlpQ antibodies add.
Match leptospirosis specimens to the week of illness (blood first, urine from week two, paired sera) and describe Weil disease and its limits as a diagnostic picture.

cues.text: Two invented patients. A camper is having a third bout of high fever, each lasting a few days, with about a week of feeling well in between.
A farm worker who cleaned up after a flood is on day ten of illness, now jaundiced, with rising creatinine.
Both may have a spirochete. Which specimen should the lab test, and when?

scenes.title: The corkscrew and its hidden flagella
scenes.altText: Schematic cards (Nakamura 2020; Jakab 2022). Spirochetes: long, thin, spiral or flat-wave cells whose flagella sit inside the periplasmic space (periplasmic flagella, also called endoflagella), not outside the cell. Rotation of these internal flagella drives the whole cell body; motility is an essential virulence factor and lets the cells move and spread within the host. Pathogens: Treponema pallidum (syphilis), Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), Leptospira interrogans (leptospirosis); relapsing fevers are also caused by spirochetes of the genus Borrelia. Leptospira bends its ends into a spiral or hook shape as it swims; several spirochetes swim better in gel-like polymer solutions such as mucin.

cues.text: Spirochetes are long, thin, spiral or wavy bacteria. Their flagella are hidden inside the cell, in the periplasmic space, so they are called periplasmic flagella, or endoflagella.
When these internal flagella rotate, the whole cell body turns and moves. Motility is an essential virulence factor that lets the cells spread within the host.
Spirochete pathogens include Treponema pallidum in syphilis, Borrelia burgdorferi in Lyme disease, Leptospira in leptospirosis, and the Borrelia species of the relapsing fevers.
Swimming leptospires bend their ends into a spiral or a hook. And several spirochetes swim better in gel-like fluids such as mucin.

scenes.title: Relapsing fever: catch it during the fever
scenes.altText: Relapsing-fever cards (Jakab 2022; Warrell 2019; Schwan 1996 abstract; Trevisan 2021). Louse-borne (LBRF) and tick-borne (TBRF) relapsing fever are caused by Borrelia spirochetes. TBRF: up to 12 recurrent febrile episodes of 2–7 days separated by afebrile periods of up to 10 days; relapses come from sequential antigenic variation of the outer-membrane lipoprotein (vmp), which evades antibody. During febrile episodes there is massive, microscopically visible bacteraemia: thick and thin blood films taken while the patient is febrile, stained with Giemsa, Wright, Wright-Giemsa, Field’s or Diff-Quik, or examined by dark-field. Positivity thresholds: thin film about 10^5, thick film about 10^4 spirochetes per mL. Serology: no commercial TBRF assays; cross-reactivity with Lyme Borrelia and Treponema pallidum; delayed seroconversion, so not useful acutely. GlpQ is produced by relapsing-fever Borrelia but not Lyme Borrelia; Lyme and syphilis sera did not react with it, but it is shared among relapsing-fever species, including B. miyamotoi.

cues.text: Relapsing fever is caused by Borrelia spirochetes spread by lice or ticks. In the tick-borne form, fever bouts of two to seven days return up to twelve times, with afebrile gaps of up to ten days.
The fever relapses because the Borrelia keep switching their outer-membrane lipoprotein, the variable membrane protein, staying one step ahead of the antibodies.

During a fever bout the blood is full of spirochetes. Take thick and thin blood films while the patient is febrile and stain them with Giemsa or Wright, or use dark-field. A thick film detects lower numbers than a thin one.

Serology is not useful acutely: antibodies come late and cross-react with Lyme Borrelia and Treponema pallidum. Antibodies to GlpQ point to relapsing-fever Borrelia, because Lyme Borrelia do not make GlpQ.

scenes.title: Leptospirosis: blood first, then urine
scenes.altText: Leptospirosis timeline (Haake 2015; Sykes 2022; Goarant 2016). Reservoir animals carry leptospires in the kidneys and shed them in urine; the brown rat is the most important source. Leptospiraemic phase: leptospires in blood, beginning before symptoms and usually declining by the end of the first week; blood cultures as soon as possible; whole-blood PCR in the first week. Urine cultured from the beginning of the second week (immune phase); urine PCR after the first week. Antibody tests including the MAT are often negative in the first week; IgM becomes detectable during the first week; paired sera with a fourfold or greater rise confirm; MAT read by dark-field. Weil disease: jaundice plus renal failure; the hemorrhage-jaundice-renal triad is under one-third of confirmed cases; severe pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome fatality >50%; case fatality <5% to >30% depending on presentation and care. Scenario answers: A, blood films during a fever bout; B, urine and paired serology.

cues.text: Leptospires live in the kidneys of reservoir animals, above all the brown rat, and are shed in urine. In humans they circulate in the blood first, until about the end of the first week, so send blood early: culture or PCR.

From the second week, culture or PCR urine instead. Antibody tests are often negative in week one, so collect paired sera. A fourfold rise in the microscopic agglutination test, read by dark-field, confirms.
Weil disease is a severe form with jaundice and kidney failure. Severe lung hemorrhage carries a death rate above fifty percent, yet most infections in endemic areas are mild or silent.
So, patient A: blood films during a fever bout. Patient B, on day ten: urine culture or PCR, plus paired serology.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A smear in the afebrile gap rules out relapsing fever” (✓ films taken during a febrile episode, when spirochetes flood the blood); “Day-10 leptospirosis: blood culture is the best specimen” (✓ leptospiraemia usually declines by the end of week one; culture urine from the start of week two and collect paired sera); “No jaundice and no biphasic fever: not leptospirosis” (✓ the Weil triad is under one-third of confirmed cases and the biphasic fever is not systematically seen).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative smear between fevers rules out relapsing fever. No: films must be taken during a fever bout.
Trap two: on day ten of leptospirosis, blood culture is best. No: by then, culture urine and collect paired sera.
Trap three: no jaundice and no two-phase fever means no leptospirosis. No: most confirmed cases lack the classic Weil picture, and the two-phase fever is not always seen.

cues.text: Memory aid: catch the corkscrew where it is. Relapsing fever lives in the blood while the fever burns. Leptospires are in the blood in week one and the urine from week two. And GlpQ is the relapser’s badge that Lyme Borrelia never wear.

Where it breaks: low spirochete numbers can be missed on a smear, GlpQ is shared among relapsing-fever species so it cannot name the species, and leptospirosis timing depends on an accurate date of symptom onset.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Relapsing fever: thick and thin blood films during a fever bout · GlpQ antibodies point to relapsing-fever Borrelia”, “Leptospirosis: blood in week 1 · urine from week 2 · paired sera”.

cues.text: Look for relapsing-fever Borrelia in blood films taken during a fever bout, and look for leptospires in blood during the first week but in urine from the second week, with paired sera to confirm.

props.label: Relapsing fever: blood film during fever · GlpQ = relapsing-fever Borrelia
Leptospirosis: blood week 1 · urine from week 2 · paired sera

explanation.what: Plain language: spirochetes are corkscrew-shaped bacteria whose whip-like flagella are tucked inside the cell, so the whole body spins as they move. Relapsing fever brings fever bouts that come and go, and the germs swarm in the blood only while the fever is up. Leptospirosis is caught from water or soil soiled by animal urine; the germs are in the blood early and in the urine later. Scientific terms: spirochete, periplasmic flagella (endoflagella), Borrelia (relapsing-fever group), louse-borne and tick-borne relapsing fever, antigenic variation, variable membrane protein (vmp), thick and thin blood films, dark-field microscopy, GlpQ (glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase), Leptospira, leptospiremic and immune phases, microscopic agglutination test (MAT), Weil disease.
explanation.why: Relapsing-fever Borrelia switch, one after another, the version of their outer-membrane lipoprotein they express, which lets them temporarily evade the antibody response and produces recurrent fever bouts; spirochete numbers in blood are high only during febrile episodes. Leptospires circulate in blood early and are cleared from it by about the end of the first week, while they reach the kidney and can be shed in urine for weeks; antibodies appear later, so early serology is often negative.
explanation.measure: Relapsing fever: thick and thin blood films (Giemsa, Wright, Wright-Giemsa, Field’s, Diff-Quik) or dark-field, taken while febrile; thin film detects about 10^5 and thick about 10^4 spirochetes per mL; serology not useful acutely; GlpQ antibodies indicate relapsing-fever Borrelia. Leptospirosis: blood culture as soon as possible and whole-blood PCR in week one; urine culture or PCR from the second week; IgM detectable during week one; paired sera with a fourfold MAT rise confirm; MAT read by dark-field.
explanation.differs: Relapsing fever (blood film during fever; recurring bouts from antigenic variation) vs leptospirosis (blood then urine; paired serology); GlpQ (relapsing-fever Borrelia) vs Lyme Borrelia, which lack it; periplasmic flagella of spirochetes vs the external flagella of bacteria such as Escherichia coli.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: best specimen and timing for relapsing fever, why an afebrile smear can be negative, what GlpQ distinguishes, which leptospirosis specimen to send in week one vs week two, how paired sera confirm, and Weil disease as a severe icteric-renal form.

questions.stem: A patient has had three bouts of high fever, each lasting a few days, separated by about a week of feeling well. Relapsing fever is suspected. Which test gives the fastest diagnosis?

options.text: Thick and thin blood films (or dark-field) on blood drawn during a febrile episode
options.rationale: Correct. Spirochetes flood the blood during febrile episodes, so films taken then are the diagnostic method of choice.

options.text: Blood films on blood drawn in the afebrile interval
options.rationale: Incorrect. Spirochete numbers are high during fevers; a film taken between bouts can miss them.
Incorrect. Seroconversion is delayed and assays cross-react, so serology does not diagnose acute infection.

options.text: Urine culture from the second week of illness
options.rationale: Incorrect. Urine culture from week two is the leptospirosis approach, not relapsing fever.

questions.stem: Antibodies to the GlpQ protein are detected in a patient’s serum. What does this most suggest?

options.text: Exposure to relapsing-fever Borrelia rather than Lyme Borrelia
options.rationale: Correct. GlpQ is produced by relapsing-fever Borrelia but not by Lyme Borrelia; Lyme and syphilis sera did not react with it.

options.text: Infection with Borrelia miyamotoi rather than other relapsing-fever species
options.rationale: Incorrect. GlpQ is shared by relapsing-fever species, so it cannot identify the species.
Incorrect. Syphilis sera were nonreactive with GlpQ.
Incorrect. GlpQ serology is used for relapsing-fever Borrelia; leptospirosis is diagnosed with tests such as the MAT on paired sera or IgM detection.

questions.stem: A farm worker on day 10 of a febrile illness after flood clean-up is suspected of leptospirosis. Which specimen plan fits best?

options.text: Urine culture or PCR, plus an acute serum with a convalescent serum 1–2 weeks later
options.rationale: Correct. Urine is cultured from the beginning of the second week, and paired sera showing a fourfold rise confirm the diagnosis.

options.text: Blood culture only, because leptospiremia peaks in the second week
options.rationale: Incorrect. Leptospiremia usually declines by the end of the first week.

options.text: A single MAT; a negative result rules leptospirosis out
options.rationale: Incorrect. Antibody tests can be negative early, and paired sera are needed to confirm.

options.text: Blood films during the next fever spike
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is the approach for relapsing fever, not leptospirosis.

claims.note: Not taught. Schwan 1996 abstract reports a 39-kDa immunoreactive clone protein; the open sources read give week one / week two timing and a <5% to >30% overall case-fatality range, not these figures.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 61 Hit 12 presents leptospirosis as two phases with Weil disease as the severe icteric form. Goarant 2016 reports that the biphasic fever is not systematically observed (and is late when it occurs) and that the Weil triad accounts for under one-third of confirmed cases, so absence of either does not exclude leptospirosis (proposed register flag rv-lepto-biphasic-weil-context).

Ch. 61 Hit 11 gives GlpQ as a 34-kDa antigen; the Schwan 1996 abstract (read as abstract only) reports the immunoreactive GlpQ clone expressing a 39-kDa protein. The molecular size is not taught (proposed register flag rv-glpq-34kda).
